extracted.intended_audience: antiquarians, ecclesiastical historians, archaeologists, and informed general readers interested in church antiquities
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and interpretive criteria for describing, dating, and understanding medieval and post-medieval church fittings (chests, windows, mazes), with attention to form, function, decoration, and documentary evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Caution: roughness of carpentry not definitive evidence of great antiquity
rubrics_metrics.description: Rough coffers formed of a single log, hollowed out, and bound with iron bands have been claimed as Norman or Saxon, but 'Roughness of design and work are scarcely, however, in themselves sufficient evidence of great antiquity;' local causes and economics may have produced very rude workmanship much later.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not date a chest to an early period based solely on crude workmanship; consider local circumstances, availability of more elaborate work, and seek corroborating evidence (documentary records, inscriptions, style parallels).

rubrics_metrics.name: Primary design criterion: strength and security
rubrics_metrics.description: In the making of church coffers 'strength was naturally the great characteristic' aimed at—strength of structure for durability and strong locks and bolts to protect contents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess structural features (thickness, joints), metalwork (iron bands, straps, hasps, multiple locks, bars), and internal partitions (e.g., separate compartments with separate locks) as indicators of priority placed on security; detailed locking arrangements (multiple hasps locking each other, bars secured by a central lock) strongly indicate security-first design and can suggest function and period.

rubrics_metrics.name: Decorative features as dating and status indicators
rubrics_metrics.description: Many chests combine solidity with 'artistic beauty'—carving, traceried panels, figures, inlays, painted colour, and metal ornamentation appear on examples from Decorated and Perpendicular periods.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use stylistic features (traceried arches, Tudor roses, crockets, figures, heraldic shields, inlay patterns) and decorative motifs to place a chest in a stylistic period (e.g., Early English, Decorated, Perpendicular) and to infer the patronage or status of the church; note also evidence of original colouring or metalwork which may survive and corroborate dating.

rubrics_metrics.name: Form indicates function: cope-chests triangular shape
rubrics_metrics.description: Copes, being large, frequently had a special receptacle; ancient cope-chests are triangular in shape because 'the cope being most easily folded into that form.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Infer intended use from form: a triangular chest likely held copes/large vestments; compare shape to liturgical needs when classifying a chest's original function.

rubrics_metrics.name: Alms-box identification by physical adaptation for coins
rubrics_metrics.description: Some coffers or parts were used as alms boxes; evidence includes a slit cut in the lid and a till or trough beneath to receive money (examples: Llanaber, Hatfield, Combs Church).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for coin-slits, tills, pierced lids, or till-compartments when identifying alms usage; presence of such adaptations is functional evidence distinct from general storage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpreting carved or carved dates with caution
rubrics_metrics.description: An inscribed or carved date (e.g., 1599) may mark repairs or alterations rather than original manufacture: 'the date perhaps marking the time of some repairs or alterations made in it.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat carved dates as terminus ante quem/terminus post quem clues—verify with stylistic, documentary, or other physical evidence before assigning original manufacture date.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provenance and documentary evidence required to corroborate physical features
rubrics_metrics.description: Examples have been moved for safety (e.g., to Newcastle castle) or repurposed; records (donor inscriptions, parish records) and local tradition help establish provenance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Combine physical examination with documentary sources (gifts, visitation records, removal during war) and local tradition to build a provenance; do not rely on present location alone because chests were sometimes removed or repurposed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not generalize from singular visual representations
rubrics_metrics.description: A mural showing a leper communicating through a window may reflect an exceptional instance: 'the very fact of the representation itself would seem to indicate rather an exceptional instance, or special circumstance.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat depicted scenes as possible special cases rather than proof of widespread practice; seek corroborating architectural, documentary, or statistical evidence before broad conclusions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpreting low-side/'lychnoscope' windows: practical positional criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: Arguments against the 'leper window' theory include that administration through such windows would often be 'exceedingly difficult, if not impossible, on account of the position' of the window; the windows are shuttered and without glass; in many cases they occur on both sides of the chancel.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing the purpose of a low-side window, consider shuttering/no glass, exact position relative to stalls and priest's door, whether a book-ledge corbel exists on the east jamb, and practical visibility to the churchyard; such spatial and physical details help differentiate functions (e.g., leper communication vs burial office use).

rubrics_metrics.name: Lych/Lych(Lych) or 'Lych Window' hypothesis: burial-use criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: The 'Lych Window' (or 'Lych Window') hypothesis posits windows used for burial offices: the priest could 'from his stall ... see the funeral cortege come into the churchyard, and then say the first part of the office through this window; which was always shuttered and without glass.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Support burial-use interpretation if the window faces principal churchyard approach, sits adjacent to priest's door or stall end, has a corbelled book-ledge, and matches local burial patterns (e.g., dominant north or south burial areas).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of proximity and siting to infer maze function
rubrics_metrics.description: English turf mazes are 'almost invariably close to a church, or the ancient site of a church,' suggesting ecclesiastical origin and devotional/penitential use rather than purely pastoral pastime.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate maze purpose by location: closeness to church or consecrated sites, presence of chapels or dedications (St. Anne, St. Catherine), and comparison with continental church labyrinths (Christian symbols, central cross) points toward devotional use; remote or purely landscape-garden siting suggests secular/topiary use.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish maze types by design and intended experience
rubrics_metrics.description: Ecclesiastical/turf labyrinths typically test patience rather than ingenuity—'there is but one road to follow'—whereas topiary mazes are 'often made purposely puzzling and misleading.' Continental church labyrinths are often inlaid marble with Christian symbols.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Classify a maze by its pattern (single continuous pathway vs multi-branching dead-ends), material (turf trenches, inlaid marble, hedge walls), and presence of liturgical markers or stations; single-thread turf mazes with ritual stations indicate penitential/pilgrimage function, while hedge mazes indicate amusement and deliberate puzzlement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpretation of local names with skepticism
rubrics_metrics.description: Local names like 'Troy Town' and 'Julian's Bower' are often later appellations and can 'imply very erroneous ideas as to their origin and purpose;' the name may post-date the construction and not indicate classical origin.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not assume ancient or classical derivation from local or popular names alone; corroborate with physical, documentary, or stylistic evidence before inferring origins from toponymy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for loss and survivorship bias in the corpus
rubrics_metrics.description: Many chests and mazes have disappeared (destroyed, ploughed up, stolen, or repurposed), and fine examples may have been removed for domestic use or lost in iconoclasm, so the surviving sample is biased.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When making generalizations about frequency, design, or chronology, adjust for survivorship and historical events (Revolution, Commonwealth iconoclasm, agricultural enclosure) that selectively removed certain classes of examples; look for documentary traces of now-lost items.
